entities.name: George Montagu, 4th Duke of Manchester
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
George Montagu, 4th Duke of Manchester (1737–1788), emerged as a prominent British Whig politician and diplomat during a tumultuous period of imperial realignment, most notably serving as Great Britain's ambassador to France in 1783. His career, spanning the latter half of the 18th century, was inextricably linked to the American Revolutionary War and its aftermath, culminating in his pivotal role in negotiating the Treaty of Paris. As a peer and member of the Privy Council, Montagu represented a faction of the British aristocracy grappling with the decline of the First British Empire and the rise of new geopolitical realities.

Before his diplomatic apotheosis, Montagu served as a Member of Parliament for Huntingdonshire from 1761 until he inherited the dukedom in 1762. Elevated to the House of Lords, he became a vocal opponent of Lord North's administration and its policies concerning the American colonies, aligning himself with the Whig opposition led by figures like Charles James Fox. Following the collapse of North's government in 1782, Montagu was appointed Lord Chamberlain of the Household and sworn into the Privy Council. His most significant appointment came in 1783 when he was dispatched to Paris as the plenipotentiary responsible for concluding the peace negotiations with France and the newly independent United States, formally signing the Treaty of Paris on September 3, 1783, alongside David Hartley.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: George Montagu's role as the British signatory of the Treaty of Paris (1783) formally ended the American Revolutionary War, establishing the United States as an independent nation and profoundly reshaping the British Empire's geopolitical standing. His actions directly contributed to the formation of the modern international system.
